case_name: P.B. v. Jewish Family & Child Services
text:
Ontario Superior Court of Justice

P.B. v. Jewish
Family & Child Services

Date:
2005-05-31

P.B. for himself

Ms Currie for Defendant

Somers J.

(orally):

[
1
]

In this case the plaintiff brings action
claiming damages against the Jewish Family and Children Services,
("Services") claiming that the manner in which they took into
protection his two children was highhanded, illegal and biased against him to
the extent that it subjected him to the forced separation from his sons and
extreme mental anguish. The position taken by services is that at all times
they acted properly and entirely within the powers and responsibilities granted
to them by the province and in no way exceeded their authority or treated the
plaintiff negligently or unfairly.

[
2
]

The plaintiff was unrepresented and testified on
his own behalf. The mother of his children is L.T. He is not married to her.
She had been previously married and had three children of that marriage, two of
them were living with her and the plaintiff during part of the time in
question. They were S.T., age 20 and J.T. age 17. The two children of his
relationship with Ms L.T. are T.B. born 1998 and N.B. born 1999. At one time
they were all living in an apartment but they moved out of that to [address
omitted] in Richmond Hill. This house was apparently in some state of disrepair
but Mr. P.B. regarded it as a temporary dwelling because he was building a
house at Musselman's Lake at a property he owned. At the time of the incident
which gave rise to this matter he was working seven days a week either as a
builder or a contractor on various jobs from which he derived an income or by
himself working on building the house at Musselman's Lake.

[
3
]

Relations between the plaintiff and his wife's
son S.T. were somewhat strained. The plaintiff was unhappy that S.T. had no
particular desire to look for a job and was around the house a good deal. Often
friends of his were at the house, including his girlfriend who was there a
considerable amount. The plaintiff said that on one occasion he was tired
having worked hard all that week and was annoyed to find this girl around the
house again. He told her he wanted her to go home and in, the course of doing
so pushed her out of the door. An argument developed between him, the
girlfriend and S.T. in which Ms L.T. participated. The result of this
altercation was that the plaintiff was charged with three counts of assault but
was released on his own recognizance. One of the conditions of his bail was
that he would move out of the house and would refrain from harassing his common
law wife. Ms L.T. had alleged that the plaintiff hit her in this dispute and
that in the course of the scuffle he stepped on one of the boy's feet and
injured him.

[
4
]

About one and a half months later after living
with his brother the plaintiff moved back into the house on [address omitted].
He says this was at the invitation of Ms L.T. In his evidence he was inclined
to disregard or minimize the fact that he was technically in breach of the
terms of his recognizance. He more than once expressed the view that the
assault really never took place. He made that statement, for example, to Susan
Sonshine a child protection worker for the defendant. By the time she was
involved with the plaintiff there had been a second altercation which he was
inclined also to treat very lightly.

[
5
]

After the first altercation the remaining two
older children of Ms L.T. moved out, wishing to be more centrally located in
the city. She invited the plaintiff's brother A.B., his wife and their two
children to come and live with them at [address omitted]. This was at about the
same time as she "allowed" the plaintiff to return. Before he moved
back in Ms L.T. told him that she had already been in touch with the defendant
service. He stated that this upset him, primarily because his wife was born
Catholic and he is of the Eastern Orthodox faith. Although her first husband was
Jewish he felt she had never evinced any interest in practising that faith
after she and the plaintiff began their relationship nor did she ever suggest
that their boys T.B. and N.B. being raised as Jews.

[
6
]

On May 20th, 2001 the police received a call from
Ms L.T. from her residence at [address omitted]. She complained that she had
received threats from her brother-in-law and sister-in-law and she wanted the
police to remove them from the house. Mr. P.B.'s version was that L.T. at this
time had seemed to be in a very mean mood trying to pick a fight with everybody
for a few days. One day he said she "went berserk". There had been a
scuffle. Ms L.T. claimed she had been beaten up. This was included in the
information she later gave to Susan Sonshine at the Service. It was clear from
what was said that there had been considerable drinking on the part of both Mr.
P.B. and Ms L.T., and loud fighting all of which had apparently taken place in
front of the children.

[
7
]

There had been a home visit by Ms Sonshine
earlier on April the 27th, 2001. She had noted that the concrete steps leading
out of the front door were crumbling, some steps missing and apparently
somewhat unsafe to be used. By this time the Service was aware that there had
been three assault charges against the plaintiff. One by his wife, one by his
stepson and one by his stepson's girlfriend. They were aware that this had
taken place in the presence of the two young children. They were aware that
there was a term of his recognizance that he was to vacate the house and not to
harras his wife but that he was back in the house. They were aware that there
had been drinking. He made the statement that he drank between 6 and 12 beers a
day. They were aware that there had been allegations of some anti-semitic
remarks made by him.

[
8
]

Ms Sonshine testified that she noticed in the
home a fireplace in the centre of the living room which caused her some concern
because there was not an adequate fire screen to cover the whole width of the
fire. At that time she was told that it had been Ms L.T.'s plan to move back in
with her ex-husband. This changed on May the 14th however, when she advised
"Services" that S.T. and J.T. had already gone there and that she was
going to stay in the house with the plaintiff who had already returned. The
plaintiff's brother, his wife and two children were also there. She expressed
some discomfort with this situation, but according to the plaintiff it was she
not he who had invited them to join them.

[
9
]

On May 21st Ms L.T. called the emergency line at
"Services" and told them that her sister-in-law had assaulted her and
she felt unsafe for herself and the children. On May 22nd two Family Service
workers conducted a home visit. They were Emma Blendis and Lynne Mortimer. They
were to report that Ms L.T. was screaming loudly, complaining of having been
hit. One of the children, N.B., was on the couch also screaming and crying.
Another child was paying no attention sitting on the floor playing with a toy.
A third child, Mrs. L.T.'s youngest was holding his ears in an attempt not to
have to listen to what was going on. The screaming was taking place in another
room and it was easy for the workers to find those people who were involved. It
was taking place in the bathroom down the hall from where the children were
located.

[
10
]

The workers noticed a bite mark on N.B.'s
shoulder apparently of fairly recent origin. When this was drawn to the
attention of the plaintiff he stated that had bathed the boy the night before
and he never noticed it. The workers both noticed old bruises on T.B.'s legs
and when they went to examine him further and asked him to draw down his
trousers he apparently thought he was going to be spanked and started to scream
"no spank, no spank". I take from the manner in which the testimony
of the plaintiff went in and his cross-examination, he is a believer in
corporal punishment for children.

[
11
]

During the course of this visit the workers
suggested that the boys should be taken to the hospital for examination. This
apparently angered the plaintiff extensively. He testified that he had thought
the people were coming to the house just for a house visit, and he blamed the
decision to take the boys to the hospital on Ms L.T. Another loud argument
developed between the two of them again in the presence of the boys. It was the
evidence of both the case workers that they felt there was a necessity, that it
was a situation which required the boys to be examined at the hospital.

[
12
]

Testimony from the case workers indicated that
when the boys were at the hospital they were virtually out of control. They
were running around, they banged on the soft drink dispenser, knocked over some
plants, and ran in and out of the examining rooms and down to the elevator. It
was apparent to both of the workers that the parents had little if any control
on the boys.

[
13
]

The emergency room notes filed as exhibits
dealing with both boys indicate no serious injuries. There were bruises on both
of them, particularly on T.B., and the bite marks on N.B. The examining doctor
indicated that they were the sort of marks that might well have caused him to
call the Children's Aid Society. The case workers felt that given the apparent
lack of supervision, the very volatile situation at home with violent arguments
taking place in front of the children they were justified in seeking a
protection order for the children under Part 3 of the Child and Family Services
Act. This step was taken after consultation with their supervisor by telephone.
The factors that they took into account was in particular the almost
out-of-control fighting and screaming that was being carried on in the presence
of the children, the apparent lack of control, the apparent lack of concern and
the evidence of some physical harm.

[
14
]

After a lengthy wait at the hospital while the
boys were examined, the children were taken by the Children's Aid workers away
with them. Their evidence was that they did not do so before telling the
parents that they were taking the children, and that they would be launching
proceedings immediately in court for a protection order. According to the
evidence Ms L.T. indicated at this time that that was all right with her
"as long as the children are safe". Mr. P.B.'s testimony was to the
effect that this took him completely by surprise, that it was done without his
being advised beforehand, and that he had not contemplated anything of the sort
when he had in effect been in agreement only that there be a home visit.

[
15
]

The first aspect of the defendant's activities
with which the plaintiff took issue was the actual taking of the boys into
protective custody. It is not in dispute as the witness Bernie Finnigan, the
supervisor of Child Protection Services testified, that the defendant qualifies
as a Children's Aid Society within the meaning of the Child Family Services
Act, 1990 R.S.O.
Chapter C-1
. Section 15.3 of the Act reads in part as follows:

The functions of a Children's Aid Society
are to:

(a) investigate allegations or evidence that children who are under
the age of 16 years or are in the Society's care or under its supervision may
be in need of protection;

(b) to protect where necessary children who are under the age of 16
years who are in the Society's care or under its supervision;

(c) provide guidance, counselling and other services to families for
protecting children or for the prevention of circumstances requiring the
protection of children;

(d) provide care for children assigned to its care under this Act.

Generally the determination of whether or
not a child needs protection requires the approval of the court. Section 40(1)
of the Act reads:

The society may apply to the court to
determine whether a child is in need of protection.

However, Section 40(7) reads as follows:

A child protection worker who believes on
reasonable and probable grounds that

(a) a child is in need of protection

(b) that there would be a substantial risk of the child's health or
safety during the time necessary to bring the matter on for a hearing under
subsection 47(1)(14) or obtain a warrant. Under sub section (2) may without a
warrant bring the child to a place of safety.

[
16
]

The Act does not specify what steps the case
worker or case workers must take before satisfying themselves that the child is
in need of protection. A useful case to take into consideration is a decision
of
Children's Aid Society of Durham (Region) v. W. (K.)
(1990),
1990 CanLII 7010 (ON PROVCT)
, 72 O.R.
(2d) 711 (Ont. Fam. Ct.). In this case Judge Webster
conducted a lengthy hearing based upon allegations made by the children that
members of the family were practising Satanism. The case was ultimately
dismissed and there was issue as whether or not the Children's Aid Society
should pay costs. This in turn depended upon whether or not the Society had
acted negligently or in bad faith. Judge Webster suggested the following
guidelines:

(a) did the Society conduct a thorough investigation before acting.

(b) did it work with the police on any abuse investigation.

(c) did it consider alternative measures for the protection of the
children before proceeding to court.

(d) did it treat both parents fairly and equally.

(e) did it ensure its workers were skilled in the performance of
their rules.

[
17
]

Although matters appeared to move very quickly
once the decision was made to have a home visit, I am of the view their
investigation was quite thorough. The workers interviewed both parents, they
attended at the home on more than one occasion and talked with both mother and
father, they received substantial background information, they arranged for the
children to be taken to the hospital to be examined, and they made copious
notes of the behaviour of both parents, particularly as the loud and violent
argument between them carried on in the presence of the children. The
Children's
Aid Society of Durham (Region) v. W. (K.)

case was adopted with approval in
the Superior Court in the case of
B. (D.) v. Children's Aid Society of
Durham (Region),
[1994] O.J. No. 643 (Ont. Gen. Div.)
, affirmed (1996),
1996 CanLII 1067 (ON CA)
, 136 D.L.R. (4th) 297 (Ont. C.A.). In that case no notification was
given to the father at all of the protection hearing at which a determination
that he had sexually abused his daughters was made. A very strict access order
was made against him after it was held. All of this was done without his
receiving any notice or even being aware that this was taking place. In the
case at Bar, the social workers indicated that the parents did not dispute
there being a protection order, and made it clear that they were going to
proceed to seek the order from the court. Moreover, it appears that both
parents were kept advised at all times of all steps that were going to be
taken.

[
18
]

The first appearance in court was May 28th, 2001
before His Honour Judge Nelson. He made an order for interim custody with
supervised access to the parents. It is important to note that the endorsement
indicates that this order was made on consent. Filed in the court at that time
was a statement of agreed facts signed by both the mother and the plaintiff
agreeing that the following were the facts. Quoting from Exhibit 6, the
statement of agreed facts that was filed in the court reads:

On February 16th, 2001 the JFCS received a
referral from the York CAS regarding a call they had received from the York
Region police on February 12, 2001 reporting that:

(a), on January 26th, 2001 P.B. the father, was charged with three
counts of assault on his partner L.T., his stepson S.T. and S.T.'s girlfriend A.

(b) at the time of assault the three younger children were at home
and witnessed the event.

(c) during the assault P.B. took L.T. by the throat and pushed her
into a child's toy box.

(d) T.B. aged three was hurt when P.B. stepped on his foot.

[
19
]

Paragraph four of the document is interesting
since the signatures of both mother and father appear to endorse it.

We agree that the court should make a
finding that the children are in need of protection for the following reasons:

There is a risk
that the children T.B. and N.B. are likely to suffer physical harm inflicted by
the parents or caused by the parents' failure to care for, provide for,
supervise or protect the children adequately.

Paragraph five reads:

We agree that the order that would best
serve the best interest of the children is:

1. An order that T.B. and N.B. be placed in care and custody of
Jewish Family and Child Service as a society ward for a period of one month,
after which time they are to be returned to their mother's care.

One of the conditions agreed to by the
plaintiff is as follows:

(a) P.B. and L.T. to attend, participate in and complete an anger
management programme and provide documentation of their completion to the
family service worker at the Jewish Family and Child Service.

(b) P.B. and L.T. to attend, participate in and complete parenting
programmes as requested by the family worker and Jewish Family and Child
Service and provide documentation of their completion to the family service
worker at the Jewish Family and Child Service.

(f) P.B. must meet with the family service worker to discuss
parenting strategies and agree to be observed implementing these strategies.

(g) P.B. must model appropriate interactions when in conflict and
must demonstrate an ability to refrain from prejudicial comment regarding race,
religion or gender.

I should point out that at the time of the
initial hearing before Judge Nelson and when the plaintiff signed this document
he was represented by counsel. In his testimony Mr. P.B. blamed his lawyer for
recommending that he sign this document and agree to the order that was
ultimately issued. He did not pursue that any further than to say that he
certainly feels now that he should never have signed it.

[
20
]

The second aspect of the defendant's activities
with which the plaintiff took issue was the supervision and limited access that
followed. The evidence of the witnesses for the defendant made it clear that
both the plaintiff and Ms L.T. were advised that these visits would be
supervised with a view to observing how each parent interacted with the
children. Indeed, the statement of agreed facts to which Mr. P.B. signed his
name indicated that he was required to agree that he would be observed during
these access periods. There is no question from the evidence given by Mr. P.B., that from comments he made during the
course of his submissions or his cross-examination that he resented having the
worker present. The evidence of the workers who did observe him was that he
appeared to disagree with almost any suggestion they made. On one occasion he
was told that one of the boys was sick and should not be given any food. His
response was to say that he would give them food if he wanted to. During his
visits he appeared to pay most of his attention to T.B., allowing N.B. to run
wild and taking no part in trying to control him. He paid no attention, for
example, when Nichols climbed up on a high window sill and was banging against
the glass. He apparently paid no attention when it was suggested that he hold
the boys' hands while walking across a parking lot where there could be cars
being driven. He let the boys run ahead. No one was hurt but it could well have
been serious if a car had been moving at the time.

[
21
]

I found it difficult to sift through the
evidence of P.B. He was contradicted on almost all points by every other
witness with the exception of that of his brother. I found him a difficult
witness in the sense that those things which were obvious matters of concern to
the defendant's employees were dismissed lightly by him. Regarding the bite
marks on N.B. for example, he indicated he never even saw them, even though it
was the opinion of Ms Blendis that they had been there for some time and should
have been noticed at the time he was giving that boy a bath. There was evidence
from the witness Ms Blendis that on one of his visits he used a knife to cut
bread and in discussion with her he became annoyed and started to wave the
knife around very close to her in a manner which made her feel unsafe. She felt
that he often displayed anger and hostility. He treated the matter very lightly
and said it was just a butter knife. On another occasion when N.B. wrapped a
lamp cord around his neck he treated that equally lightly and said it wasn't a
lamp cord at all, it was just a slinky toy. As for N.B. banging his head on a
window, he said well it was probably very thick glass.

[
22
]

A prime source of annoyance to Mr. P.B. appears
to have been the involvement of the defendant in that it is a Jewish
organization. He is not Jewish nor is his wife, although she filed affidavit
material in the proceedings indicating that she was a convert to Judaism. Her
first husband was a Jew and apparently when they were together she managed a
kosher kitchen. She also took part in other rituals of the Jewish faith. Mr.
P.B. seemed particularly concerned about the possibility of his two sons being
circumcised.

[
23
]

My review of the earlier court proceedings makes
it clear that the trial judge did make a finding that the boys were Jewish, but
it was for the purpose of that proceeding. By this method he confirmed and
authorized the involvement of the defendant organization. I regard the scope of
that order as extending no further than that.

[
24
]

There was testimony from more than one source
that indicated that Mr. P.B. made a number of offensive anti-semitic remarks in
his home and in the offices of the Service and in conversation with the workers
while in his home. For example, to Ms Sonshine he referred to S.T. his wife's
son by her first marriage as "Jew boy", and threatened that he would
"beat the Hebrew out of him". He also said "my kids are better
than you", apparently because they were not Jewish. He made similar
comments to the receptionist at Services office, accusing them of wanting to
"cut of the ends of my boys' penises".

[
25
]

Both the parents were told by the court that in
order for them to receive back the children they should undergo anger
management and parenting courses. Mr. P.B. was delinquent in attending the
anger management course and was told he failed and would have to reattend.
Eventually he did complete it. His experience in the parenting
group was not successful. The group was to meet once a week to discuss as a
group the personal experiences of the individual members in raising children.
He missed the second meeting but attended the third armed with a tape recorder
which he turned on. This upset the other participants who, for confidentiality
reasons, did not want to have what they were saying recorded. He was asked to
turn it off and initially he argued about it and would not do so. It was only
after he had words that he stood up and according to Ms Diane Sherkin threw the
tape in her face and said "I've got what I needed", and walked out.
He then asked if he could stay since he had turned off the tape, but Ms Sherkin
refused and a male worker escorted him out of the building. He was told then
that he could restart this course with another group but he never made
arrangements to do.

[
26
]

The witness Emma Blendis noticed that when Mr.
P.B. exercised his access rights he spent most of the time playing with T.B.
and letting N.B. run wild, paying little or not attention to him. He climbed up
on the furniture and one occasion as I have indicated wrapped a lamp cord
around his neck.

[
27
]

It is not part of this court's function to
determine whether or not the results reached by the judge or judges hearing
various earlier aspects of this matter were properly arrived at, nor would I
quarrel with them in the event. It was always open to Mr. P.B. to appeal any of
these decisions if he was dissatisfied with them. I am satisfied that the
actions taken by the social workers in gathering together the information,
making the home visits, attending at the hospital and talking to the treating
doctors, making the decision that an application should be made to bring the
children into custody, filing the material in court as and when it became
available, and subsequently supervising the access by both parents was fair and
more than adequate. I accept the evidence of Susan Son-shine, Emma Blendis and
Diane Sherkin over that of the plaintiff in any part where it contradicts that
of the plaintiff. I do not consider his claim in the statement of claim that
the attitude of the workers from the Family Services were malicious or
adversarial, or that the protection order they obtained was completely and
totally inappropriate and unnecessary, or that the workers who handled the
matter were incompetent or negligent".

[
28
]

I am conscious of the broad powers granted to
children's aid societies in these situations can be abused or biased. The power
to take away the children of a citizen is one that must always be exercised
with extreme care and sensitivity. I believe that in this case this was done. I
am also conscious that in the exercise of these powers the sensitivities of the
parents can be deeply bruised. Clearly those of Mr. P.B. were seriously
affected. I fear, however, that he has allowed his judgment to be clouded by
what has happened and persuaded him to make the broad and strong accusations
which at times bordered on the scurrilous. I do, however, express the hope that
now that this family is reunited since September of 2004 it will live in
something much closer to harmony. It follows from what I have said that in my
view this action should be dismissed and I so order.

[
29
]

I have reviewed the statements of claim and make
brief comments about the other apparent causes of action contained in it. There
is in paragraph 20 a claim which although not specifically worded appears to be
a derivative claim similar to one made under the Family Law Act. Such a claim
requires for its existence the presence of a claim made specifically on behalf
of children or other members of a family. This was not done and so that claim
must therefore fail. Similarly, with respect to any claim made on behalf of the
children for injury or damages, this was not properly pleaded nor was there any
evidence advanced of any harm to the children apart from the fact that one of
the boys was burned by a curling iron in the home of one of the foster homes.
The circumstances of that particular injury were not gone into. Finally, there
is a claim alleging that the defendant service owes a fiduciary duty to the
plaintiff. I disagree with that. It owes a fiduciary duty, if at all, to the
children and in any view as I have held, it exercised that duty properly and in
accordance with professional principles. Under all the heads of damages claimed
in this action therefore, the case is dismissed.

Action dismissed.
